content: It is not feasible to provide comprehensive care, whether physical or psychosocial, for both patients and their families in a hospital setting. When patients and staff are in the same location, training and education are more easily facilitated. Donors can directly observe the impact of their contributions, and volunteers can gather, fostering a stronger sense of community and belonging. However, highly skilled medical and nursing care, if offered, represents the most expensive form of palliative care, potentially costing as much or more than hospital care. Patients often prefer to receive care or pass away in their own homes rather than in a hospice. Practical challenges such as distance, cost, or convenience may limit the frequency of family visits. Additionally, if a hospice experiences a high number of deaths, it may unsettle patients and lead to the facility being stigmatized as a death house. Hospice day-care services allow patients to remain in their homes while receiving specialized care at a hospice during the day. This arrangement can provide custodial care for patients while family members are at work, enabling patients to stay at home until they are no longer able to travel. Transportation, such as ambulances equipped with wheelchair facilities or stair crawlers, may be required unless families can transport the patient themselves. Travel time and distance can be limiting factors, and patients may arrive at the day-care center already fatigued. Group activities offered in such settings may not be suitable for all patients. Education centers benefit from having patients concentrated in one location, providing ample clinical material for teaching purposes. Groups of trainees can be accommodated if appropriate facilities are available. However, the privacy of patients and their families must be safeguarded. Clinical staff involved in teaching may need a reduced workload, and employing trained teaching staff incurs additional costs. Research centers attract high-caliber staff due to their academic culture, but research requires significant investment in time and money. Most clinicians are not trained in research and require additional training. Dedicated time and staff are essential for conducting research. Palliative care centers or hospices must clearly define the types of patients they will accept, as this determines the care provided. For example, some centers may focus on cancer patients, while others may cater to individuals with HIV/AIDS, strokes, or dementia. Decisions must also be made regarding whether to accept children, adults, or both. The prognosis of patients may also influence the focus of care, whether it is based on survival and recovery or solely on the need for palliative care. Admission and discharge criteria are essential, and mechanisms should be in place for patients to return to the hospice program during crises. Geographical location is particularly important for home care, as travel time for staff limits the catchment area. For inpatient hospice care, accessibility for visiting family members may also be a limitation. Technology, such as mobile and computer-based tools, can support patients in rural and remote areas. Socioeconomic conditions of patients may influence the setup of palliative care centers, with some focusing on serving the very poor or homeless. While universal coverage is the goal, limited resources may constrain care for all. Family involvement varies, with some centers allowing family members to stay with the patient, while others permit only visits. Decisions must also be made regarding the maximum number of guests allowed per patient. Before establishing a palliative care service, clarity is needed on the mix of paid staff and volunteers, as well as the expertise required from professional staff. Needs vary depending on the type of service provided. For home care, nurses often act as primary care managers, calling in other resources as needed. In resource-rich settings, interdisciplinary teams with coordinators are common. Special training in symptom assessment and case management is essential for nursing staff. In inpatient services, nursing staff with varying levels of expertise must be available 24/7, forming the largest group within the interdisciplinary team. Day-care services may be managed by occupational therapists, physiotherapists, or nurse managers, with medical input depending on available resources. Specialists in palliative care or general physicians with some training in palliative care may provide medical input. Centers of excellence and training require highly trained palliative care specialists, and joint appointments or service-level agreements may be necessary to address recruitment challenges. Medical social workers and counselors are integral to the interdisciplinary hospice team. Junior staff with limited clinical experience may require mentoring from experienced workers. Allied health professionals, such as occupational, physiotherapy, and speech therapists, may be needed part-time or full-time and require training in managing patients with advanced diseases. Volunteers play a vital role in hospice services, enriching care and often forming the backbone of manpower. However, training and coordination are necessary, and volunteers are not without cost. Beyond patient care, volunteers can assist with governance, fundraising, awareness campaigns, and administrative tasks. The reliable availability of essential medications, particularly oral morphine, is critical for pain and symptom management. In many countries where palliative care is underdeveloped, such medications are only available in hospitals, necessitating collaboration with hospital staff to provide them for home or hospice patients. Training in the appropriate use of controlled medicines is crucial to ensure prescribers are confident and free from unnecessary fears. Funding for palliative care services may come from foundations, public donations, legacies, government subsidies, co-payments by end-users, or a combination of these sources. Many palliative care centers begin as community projects funded by charitable organizations. For sustainability, government funding should be sought to cover part or all of the services provided, as the goal is to integrate palliative care into the health system. Public fundraising is also beneficial, promoting community awareness and ownership. In some regions, such as Kerala, India, micro-donations from the public form the primary funding source for palliative care services, supplemented by government support. In Costa Rica, palliative care facilities are financed by public funds, with state establishments receiving budgets from social security and additional funding from national lotteries. Independent units are supported by civil society organizations. Many programs are also backed by associations or foundations that raise funds for patient care. External support plays a role in training, funding, and workforce development in lowand middle-income countries where palliative care services are not yet established. Initiatives such as training-of-trainers programs, overseas clinical fellowships, embedding trained professionals in local units, and seed funding for services are valuable. However, sustainability from local resources must be prioritized from the outset. The integration of palliative care services requires coordination across all levels of the health system to ensure seamless transitions for patients and families. There is no universal approach to integration, as it depends on existing services. However, general principles for success include respecting district health service values, being dynamic and responsive to needs, and fostering co-production and shared knowledge about palliative care.
